newsitem.title: UK: British army tackles IRA bomb, Sinn Fein seeks talks.
newsitem.headline: British army tackles IRA bomb, Sinn Fein seeks talks.

text.p: British army bomb disposal experts on Monday examined a huge Irish Republican Army (IRA) bomb which the guerrillas abandoned at the Northern Irish town of Strabane on the first anniversary of their broken 17-month ceasefire.

As the army tackled the device, a spokesman for Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, said its leadership had written to British Prime Minister John Major seeking to set up a meeting between the party and British officials about a new IRA truce.
Britain has banned all contact with Sinn Fein, which shares the IRA's goal of ending British rule of Northern Ireland to reunite it with the Irish republic, until the IRA halts violence.
The spokesman told Reuters that Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams had written to Major asking him to drop the ban so that Sinn Fein and British officials could hold exploratory talks.

On Sunday British officials said the ban remained in force but they left open the possibility of contacts with Sinn Fein if the IRA halted attacks on police and troops which its has mounted every week this year.

Sinn Fein wants clarification about the conditions under which a new IRA truce might allow it to enter all-party peace talks in Belfast, from which it is barred because of the latest IRA campaign, which began on February 9 last year.

Britain says Sinn Fein could not join other parties at the talks until it is satisfied that any new IRA truce is permanent but Sinn Fein says it should be invited to the negotiations without any preconditions.
Adams has repeatedly called on Major to act on Northern Ireland before an election, which is due by May, to give the Northern Ireland peace process new impetus.

The device abandoned at Strabane was the second the IRA has ditched this year, apparently because of stepped up security patrols around key targets. It left a similarly big device at a Belfast castle in January. Police said the Strabane device, which the IRA claimed to be packed with 1,000 lb (500 kilos) of explosive, could have killed many people and caused huge damage had it been detonated.
It was dumped close to a hotel with 250 guests and a housing estate at Strabane, some 50 miles (80 km) northwest of Belfast.
Security sources believe the IRA wanted to detonate it at a British security target or government building but were thwarted by security patrols.
It was left on February 9, the first anniversary of an IRA bomb attack at London's Canary Wharf business complex which marked the end of the guerrillas' cesefire.
